questions.stem: Which process divides the cytoplasm of an animal cell?

options.text: An actin and myosin ring contracts, producing a cleavage furrow
options.why: The contractile ring pulls the plasma membrane inward until the cytoplasm is divided.

options.text: Vesicles fuse at the equator and grow outward to form a cell plate
options.why: That describes cytokinesis in a plant cell. Its rigid wall prevents the membrane from being pinched inward.

options.text: Spindle microtubules shorten and divide the cytoplasm between the nuclei
options.why: Spindle microtubules move chromosomes during nuclear division. They don't divide the animal cell's cytoplasm.

options.text: The nuclear envelope constricts around the equator and separates the whole cell
options.why: The nuclear envelope encloses a nucleus. Cytokinesis depends on a contractile ring beneath the plasma membrane.

questions.stem: Why is cytokinesis unequal during human oogenesis?

options.text: One cell retains most of the cytoplasm and organelles needed for early development
options.why: The future ovum receives most of the resources, while much smaller polar bodies receive little cytoplasm.

options.text: Every meiotic product needs an equal chromosome number but a different number of genes
options.why: The cells receive haploid chromosome sets, and unequal cytokinesis doesn't give them different numbers of genes.

options.text: One nucleus remains diploid while the other nuclei become haploid polar bodies
options.why: Meiosis produces haploid nuclei. The inequality concerns the amount of cytoplasm, not retention of a diploid nucleus.

options.text: The spindle transfers every mitochondrion into the cell that becomes the ovum
options.why: Most cytoplasm and organelles enter the ovum, but the spindle separates chromosomes rather than transferring every mitochondrion.

questions.stem: What has happened to a chromosome immediately after DNA replication?

options.text: It consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere
options.why: Each chromatid contains one replicated DNA molecule. They remain joined until their scheduled separation.

options.text: It has paired with its homologous chromosome to form a permanent bivalent
options.why: Homologues associate as bivalents during meiosis I, not as a direct result of DNA replication.

options.text: Its chromosome number has doubled because each DNA molecule is counted separately
options.why: Joined sister chromatids count as one chromosome. DNA content has doubled, but chromosome number hasn't.

options.text: Its sister chromatids have already separated and moved into different daughter nuclei
options.why: Chromatid separation occurs later, during anaphase of mitosis or anaphase II of meiosis.

questions.stem: A micrograph shows two groups of sister chromatids moving toward opposite poles. Which phase is shown?

options.text: Prophase
options.why: In prophase, chromosomes condense but haven't separated into two groups.

options.text: Metaphase
options.why: In metaphase, duplicated chromosomes are aligned at the equator rather than moving apart.

options.text: Anaphase
options.why: Anaphase is identified by sister chromatids separating and moving toward opposite poles.

options.text: Telophase
options.why: In telophase, chromosomes have reached the poles and new nuclear envelopes are forming.

questions.stem: Which event makes meiosis I a reduction division?

options.text: Homologous chromosomes separate into different nuclei
options.why: Separating each homologous pair gives each nucleus one chromosome from the pair, changing diploid nuclei into haploid nuclei.

options.text: Sister chromatids separate after their centromeres divide during the first meiotic division
options.why: Sister chromatids normally remain joined during meiosis I and separate in meiosis II.

options.text: DNA replication produces half as many chromatids as the parent nucleus originally contained
options.why: Replication increases DNA content. Reduction happens later through segregation of homologous chromosomes.

options.text: Cytokinesis removes one chromosome from every homologous pair in each new cell
options.why: Nuclear division segregates the chromosomes. Cytokinesis divides cytoplasm rather than selecting chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which event directly produces recombinant chromatids during meiosis?

options.text: Exchange of corresponding DNA segments between non-sister chromatids
options.why: Crossing over between homologues combines maternal and paternal DNA within individual chromatids.

options.text: Independent orientation of every bivalent at the metaphase I equator
options.why: Random orientation changes combinations of whole maternal and paternal chromosomes. It doesn't exchange DNA between chromatids.

options.text: Random fusion of two genetically different haploid gametes during fertilization
options.why: Random fertilization adds variation to offspring, but it occurs after meiosis and doesn't create recombinant chromatids.

options.text: Separation of sister chromatids toward opposite poles during anaphase II
options.why: Anaphase II distributes chromatids that already exist. It doesn't exchange DNA between them.

questions.stem: Which event can produce a zygote with trisomy 21?

options.text: Non-disjunction produces a gamete with two copies of chromosome 21
options.why: Fusion with a normal gamete adds one more copy, giving the zygote three copies of chromosome 21.

options.text: Crossing over exchanges equal chromosome 21 segments between homologous chromosomes
options.why: Normal crossing over exchanges DNA segments without adding a whole chromosome to the gamete.

options.text: DNA replication creates sister chromatids of chromosome 21 before normal segregation
options.why: Replication before meiosis is normal. Trisomy can result when the replicated chromosomes fail to segregate correctly.

options.text: Cytokinesis gives one gamete more cytoplasm than the other meiotic products
options.why: Unequal cytoplasm doesn't alter chromosome number. Trisomy follows an error in chromosome segregation.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the correct order of the eukaryotic cell cycle?

options.text: G1, S, G2, mitosis, cytokinesis
options.why: The cell grows in G1, replicates DNA in S, continues preparation in G2, divides its nucleus and then divides its cytoplasm.

options.text: S, G1, mitosis, G2, cytokinesis
options.why: DNA replication doesn't precede initial cell growth, and G2 occurs before mitosis rather than after it.

options.text: G1, G2, S, cytokinesis, mitosis
options.why: S phase belongs between G1 and G2, and nuclear division normally precedes completion of cytokinesis.

options.text: Mitosis, G1, cytokinesis, S, G2
options.why: This places cytoplasmic division after a new growth phase. Cytokinesis follows mitosis before the next cycle begins.

questions.stem: Which observation best shows that interphase is metabolically active?

options.text: The cell synthesizes proteins, replicates DNA and increases its organelles
options.why: Interphase includes growth and biosynthesis, with DNA replication occurring specifically during S phase.

options.text: The chromosomes remain condensed while metabolism stops before nuclear division
options.why: Chromosomes are generally decondensed during interphase, and the cell remains metabolically active.

options.text: The cytoplasm divides repeatedly without any increase in cellular components
options.why: Cytokinesis isn't interphase. Cells must produce components before repeated divisions can continue.

options.text: The spindle moves homologous chromosomes while mitochondria remain unable to divide
options.why: Spindle movement occurs during nuclear division. Mitochondria can grow and divide during interphase.

questions.stem: How do cyclins control progression through the cell cycle at the level required for D2.1?

options.text: Different cyclin concentrations rise and fall, and a threshold permits passage through each checkpoint
options.why: Changing cyclin levels make cell-cycle events occur in sequence. The required threshold must be reached before a checkpoint is passed.

options.text: One cyclin remains at a constant high concentration and drives every stage continuously
options.why: Different cyclin concentrations change during the cycle. Constant stimulation would fail to provide ordered checkpoint control.

options.text: Cyclins attach to spindle microtubules and pull each chromatid through a checkpoint
options.why: Spindle machinery moves chromosomes. Cyclins regulate progression through checkpoints rather than physically moving chromatids.

options.text: Cyclins replicate DNA and repair every mutation before the cell enters interphase
options.why: Cyclins are regulatory proteins. They don't copy DNA, and interphase occurs before mitosis rather than after checkpoint completion.

questions.stem: Which change can promote uncontrolled cell division?

options.text: A proto-oncogene becomes an overactive oncogene
options.why: A proto-oncogene normally promotes division under control. Its oncogenic form can stimulate cell-cycle progression excessively.

options.text: A tumour suppressor gene becomes more effective at stopping damaged cells
options.why: Greater tumour suppressor activity would strengthen restraint. Loss-of-function mutations are the dangerous change.

options.text: Every checkpoint gains a higher cyclin threshold and becomes harder to pass
options.why: Harder checkpoint passage would tend to slow division. Cancer develops when controls that restrain proliferation are lost or bypassed.

options.text: An oncogene changes back into a normally regulated proto-oncogene in the cell
options.why: Returning to normal regulation would remove excessive stimulation rather than promote uncontrolled division.

questions.stem: A tumour has a high mitotic index and its cells invade neighboring tissue. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: It is a rapidly dividing malignant tumour
options.why: The high mitotic index indicates frequent division, while invasion identifies malignant behavior.

options.text: It is benign because rapid division prevents cells from leaving the original tissue
options.why: Invasion rules out a benign classification. Benign tumours remain localized and don't invade neighboring tissue.

options.text: It has already formed a secondary tumour because its mitotic index is high
options.why: A high mitotic index measures division, not spread. A secondary tumour requires evidence that cells established growth elsewhere.

options.text: It must have arisen in another organ and returned to its primary location
options.why: Nothing here identifies where the tumour began. A primary tumour is the original growth, while secondary tumours form after metastasis.
